# Is AI Worth It?

::: {.callout-note}

-   Restate a vague worry about AI tools ("is this helping us?") as an
    answerable research question.
-   Distinguish the *kinds* of question that call for qualitative versus
    quantitative methods.
-   Recognize why most coverage of AI-productivity studies can't be trusted
    on its own.

:::

In early 2023 a team at GitHub published a paper claiming that developers using
Copilot completed a programming task **55% faster** than those who did not
[@Peng2023]. Within weeks that number was everywhere: all-hands decks, vendor
sites, blog posts calling it a "landmark study." Executives repeated it to
justify buying tools for thousands of developers. Almost nobody asked the
question that actually mattered: *is 55% even a plausible answer to the question
I have?*

It turns out the study used 95 people doing one artificial task — building an
HTTP server in JavaScript from scratch — for ninety minutes, and it was funded
by GitHub, the company that sells Copilot. None of that makes the result
*wrong*. It does mean "55% faster" describes a very narrow slice of what your
team does all day, and it may not transfer to *your* question at all.

This workshop is about learning to answer the question your manager is going to
ask you in two weeks:

> We're paying $X per developer per year for this AI tool. Is it worth it?

That question is smaller than it looks, because every word in it is doing hidden
work. Worth *what*? To *whom*? Compared to *what alternative*? Over *what time
period*? Most of this workshop is about turning those hidden words into things
you can actually measure.

## The Running Case

To keep the ideas concrete, every chapter will return to the same situation.

Meridian is a mid-sized company that builds software for supply-chain logistics.
Three months ago it rolled out an AI coding assistant to all of its ~200
developers. The CTO now wants to know whether the subscription is paying for
itself. Four people have been asked to figure it out:

- **Maya**, a staff engineer — skeptical, wants evidence she can defend, and
  deeply suspicious of vendor numbers.
- **Dev**, the engineering manager who chose the tool — wants a clean dashboard
  metric he can show the CTO, ideally one that goes up and to the right.
- **Jonas**, a junior developer — the tool's biggest fan, who genuinely feels
  faster with it, but has the least experience to judge whether that feeling is
  right.
- **Priya**, a solutions engineer from the vendor — friendly, knowledgeable, and
  paid to keep Meridian as a customer.

Each chapter will hand this group a different way of attacking the question.
Watch for the moments where Maya, Dev, Jonas, and Priya each *feel* sure of
something — and where the methods in this book show one of them is wrong.

## Two Ways to Answer the Question

When you set out to evaluate a tool, you can do it one of two ways, and the
question — not your preference — decides which is right.

**Quantitative** methods *measure* things: how long a task takes, how many
defects ship, how many pull requests merge in a week. They answer "how much" and
"is there a difference." They only work when you can define and count the thing
you care about — which, as the next chapter shows, is harder for "productivity"
than most people admit.

**Qualitative** methods *describe* things: what developers think of the tool,
why a team adopted it and another didn't, where people get stuck. They answer
"why" and "what's actually happening." They only work when you can get close
enough to real people to see their actual experience, not their survey answers.

Neither is more rigorous than the other. A good program mixes both: qualitative
work often *finds* the right question, and quantitative work *answers* it. The
trap is methodological tribalism — "we only do numbers" or "numbers can't
capture developer experience" — which usually means the speaker would rather
not find out something that complicates a decision they've already made.

## Why You Can't Trust the Coverage

Most of what you'll read about AI and developer productivity is filtered through
several layers, each of which degrades accuracy:

-   **Journalists read abstracts.** Abstracts rarely report limitations, and the
    story "AI makes developers 55% faster" is a lot more shareable than "one
    study on one toy task found a speed-up."
-   **Press releases are marketing.** They exist to generate coverage, not
    accuracy, and they're written by people whose job is to make the funder
    look good.
-   **Preprints look just like papers.** To a non-specialist, an unreviewed
    arXiv preprint and a peer-reviewed journal article are indistinguishable —
    and a large fraction of AI-productivity studies are one, not the other.
-   **Conflict of interest is the norm.** A large share of these studies are
    funded by the companies selling the tools, so the default assumption should
    be that the deck is stacked, not that it isn't.

The lesson isn't "don't believe anything." It's *"trace the claim to the
evidence, and ask what the evidence can actually support."* That's the skill
this workshop teaches.

## Misconceptions

Peer review means a study is correct.
:   Peer review filters out obvious errors and implausible claims; it does not
    certify validity. Reviewers rarely re-run analyses or check the raw data.

A larger sample always makes a study better.
:   Sample size can't fix a flawed design. Ten thousand people doing an
    irrelevant task tell you nothing about the question you actually care about.

Qualitative methods are less rigorous than quantitative methods.
:   They use different standards of rigor, not lower ones.

One well-designed study settles a question.
:   A single study reports what happened in one sample under one set of
    conditions. Findings become trustworthy through replication across
    different samples, contexts, and teams.

## Check Understanding

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">What is the difference between a claim and evidence?</summary>

A claim is an assertion, such as "AI tools make programmers more productive."
Evidence is what a systematic study produces when it tests that claim, and it
varies in quality depending on design, sample, context, and bias. A single study
produces evidence for or against a specific claim under specific conditions; it
does not prove or disprove the claim in general.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">The GitHub Copilot study found a 55% speed increase. Dev says this means AI doubles productivity. Name two specific problems with that interpretation.</summary>

First, the study used a single artificial task, which doesn't represent the
range of work developers actually do. Second, "55% faster on one task" is not
"doubles overall productivity" — productivity includes far more than task
completion time, and the effect on the whole working day is unknown. Third, the
study was funded by GitHub, which has a financial interest in Copilot looking
effective.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">Maya wants to use numbers only; Jonas says developer experience can't be captured numerically. Who's right?</summary>

Neither. The method follows the question. "How much time does this save?" is a
quantitative question; "why do people hesitate to accept suggestions?" is a
qualitative one. Dismissing either approach before knowing the question is
methodological tribalism, not reasoning.

</details>

## Exercises

### Restate the Question (10 minutes, solo)

Meridian's CTO asks, "Are we getting our money's worth from this AI tool?" Write
down three *specific, answerable* research questions that unpack that vague
one — each with the metric you'd need, the comparison you'd make, and the time
period you'd look at. Example: "Has median time-to-first-review for pull
requests changed since we deployed the tool, compared to the three months
before?" Keep them to one sentence each.

### Qualitative or Quantitative? (10 minutes, pairs)

For each question below, say whether you'd primarily use qualitative or
quantitative methods, and in one sentence why:

-   Do developers who use the assistant produce fewer defects?
-   Why do some teams on Meridian's codebase use the tool daily while others
    ignore it?
-   How do developers decide when to trust an AI suggestion versus working it
    out themselves?
-   Does code review take less time when reviewers use the assistant?

### Spot the Gap (15 minutes, pairs)

Pick one AI-productivity claim you've actually heard (for example, "AI cuts
onboarding time in half" or "AI-generated code has more security bugs"). Find
the study behind it — or the closest thing to one — and list, in one line each:
who funded it, what the sample actually was, what task was studied, and what the
headline claims versus what the methods actually show. Compare your list with
your partner's; the point is to feel how much a headline hides.
